---
title: "Lecture: State space models"
date: 2026-10-05
---

In today's lecture Birgit introduced state space models, and this is the section I have enjoyed most so far.

**Observation equals signal plus noise.** The idea is that there is an underlying state $\theta_t$ that we never see directly, and the data $y_t$ are noisy measurements of it. Each observation depends only on the current state, and the state moves forward like a Markov chain, where the next state only depends on the one before it. The whole model is two equations:

$$Y_t = F\theta_t + v_t, \qquad v_t \sim N(0, V)$$

$$\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t, \qquad w_t \sim N(0, W)$$

The first is the observation equation and the second is the state equation. With a normal starting value for $\theta_0$ this is the dynamic linear model, and the Kalman filter is used to fit it.

**Building up three models.** I found it interesting how we built up the three models. First the local level model, where the observation is just based on the state, and the state is a level that moves as a random walk, $\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + w_t$. We fitted this to the Nile data with `statespacer`. Then we added a slope $\beta_t$ into the state, which is also a random walk, so the level can trend up or down and the trend itself can change. This is the local linear trend model, and it suited the global temperature series where the trend changes direction. Lastly we added seasonality, with seasonal effects that add up to zero over a year, which gives the basic structural model. We applied this to monthly Cape Town temperature and UK gas consumption with `StructTS`. Each new part is one more piece added to the state, and not a whole new model.

**Why I liked it.** I like how diverse this technique is, as it can be applied to many different models. ARIMA and exponential smoothing can both be written in state space form and fitted the same way. It handles missing values without any extra work, it does not need the series to be stationary, and explanatory variables can be added to the observation equation. I also found it easier to think about adding a trend or a seasonal part than to work out AR and MA orders from the ACF and PACF.

**What to watch out for.** Birgit also pointed out the downsides. The variances $V$, $W$ and the component variances can be hard to tell apart from each other, and maximising the likelihood is harder than the software makes it look, so good starting values matter. This is why the `initial` argument is needed in the `statespacer` calls.

**Link to Project 4.** This was the model I most wanted to try on real data, to see how a level that is allowed to change over time would do on a series with trend and seasonality. So I used it as the starting point to build Project 4, where I wanted to code the Kalman filter myself.

**Takeaway:** a state space model splits a series into a hidden state and noise, and more structure is added by adding pieces to the state. Because so many models fit into this one framework, it ties together a lot of what we have done so far in the course.
